w: What's tested Cavities vs notches at the gumline: the same spot, a different cause The three causes of the notches, alone or together: brushing, biting forces and acid Brushing: the toothpaste matters more than the brush; the RDA number; soft brushes, less pressure; worse on the side of the hand you brush with Why not every notch comes from brushing Biting forces (abfraction): how a push on the biting surface makes a notch at the neck of the tooth, its clues and the night guard Acid: erosion vs cavities, where throwing up does damage, pH vs buffering capacity, and the worst drinks Fix the cause, and when to fill a notch This lecture is Dr. Lawson's, recorded ahead of time for the 11/12 class. It's about noncarious cervical lesions (NCCLs): notches worn into a tooth at the gumline that aren't cavities. Cavity or not? Plaque collects at the gumline, so cavities form there too. Those look like cavities: soft and brown, and a good filling for them is resin-modified glass ionomer. NCCLs sit in the same spot but have a different cause: not decay. They can be brown too, but they look hard. There are three causes, and a notch can have one, two or all three: Abrasion: from brushing. Abfraction: from biting forces. Erosion: from acid. Brushing (abrasion) A researcher (Dzakovich) brushed pulled teeth set in fake gums and made notches like the real ones near the gum line. Brushing without toothpaste made no notches, so the toothpaste matters more than the brush. Ask what toothpaste the patient uses. A toothpaste's RDA (relative dentin abrasivity) says how scratchy it is: a higher number means more abrasive. Pick a low one; to get the ADA seal, it must be below 250. (A Colgate whitening paste is about 124; Crest Pro-Health is always high.) Still use a soft brush: it protects the gums too. Brush with less pressure; an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor helps. A clue: people press harder on the side of the hand they brush with, so brushing notches are worse on that side. Notches only on the left? Ask if the patient is left-handed. Not every notch is from brushing People with leprosy who couldn't brush their own teeth, ancient people from before toothbrushes, and animals (a camel, a cat) have had these notches. They also show up on the roof of the mouth, where people don't brush, and under the gums, where bristles can't reach. So something else causes some of them. Biting forces (abfraction) A push on the slope of a cusp bends the tooth to one side. The tooth is held in the bone, which acts as the pivot. Teeth, like most materials, handle squeezing better than stretching. The side being stretched is under tension, and that's where the notch forms, just above the bone. Think of pushing on a stop sign: it bends at the ground, and the stretched side is where it gets damaged. It's hard to tell for sure, but clues are bony bumps (tori and exostoses) and worn, matching spots on the teeth from grinding. The fix: a night guard, a piece of plastic to grind on instead of the teeth (here it isn't a treatment for jaw joint problems). Dr. Givan's L7 adds that abfraction is shown in the lab but not yet proven in patients. Acid (erosion) Cavities are acid too, but made by bacteria where plaque sits. Erosion is acid from what we eat, drink or bring up, wherever the liquid sits. Cupped-out molar tips come from wear plus acid: once the enamel wears through and the dentin underneath shows, the acid eats the dentin faster, because dentin starts to dissolve at a higher pH than enamel. Throwing up erodes the tongue side of the upper teeth: the lip protects the outside surfaces, and the tongue covers the lower teeth. Acid shows up where bacteria don't: the cusp tips, the tongue side of the upper front teeth, worn biting edges, and the cheek side where brushing has worn it. Cavities show up where plaque sits: white spots at the gumline or after braces, the grooves, and between the teeth. Drinks Talk to patients about acidic drinks, and explain pH simply (water is 7; lower is more acidic). Milk in coffee makes it less acidic, and tea beats coffee. In sparkling water, more bubbles means more acid; the brand matters more than the flavor. Buffering capacity is how much saliva (bicarbonate) it takes to neutralize a drink. Needing more is worse. pH is read with a probe; buffering capacity is measured by adding bicarbonate bit by bit until the pH is back to neutral. Measured that way, orange juice and wine are much worse than their pH alone suggests. Citric acid grabs calcium (it's a chelator), so citrus is very erosive. Safer choices: water, milk, or Milo's tea (unsweet on his slide; the sweet tea has no fermentable sugar if it's made with Splenda). Raising the pH Mouth rinses can be acidic, but you don't rinse for long, so he isn't worried about them. To raise the mouth's pH, use a base: bicarbonate, as in a baking soda rinse or Basic Bites candies (bicarbonate plus arginine). Rinsing with water, keeping acidic drinks to mealtimes and using a straw make sense but aren't proven. Water doesn't neutralize much: pH is a log scale, so you'd need a swimming pool of it. A base works. Fix the cause, then decide on a filling Find the cause first: someone who sucks on lemons all day doesn't need a toothpaste talk. Brushing: a lower-RDA toothpaste, then a pressure-sensor brush. Acid: a less acidic drink and bicarbonate. Biting forces: a night guard. You don't have to fill a notch that is easy to keep clean, doesn't hurt, looks fine and isn't deep (near the nerve). One that fails any of those gets filled.
